titolo: Egypt Is Bigger Than Texas… So Why Does Everyone Live Here?

numero.sotto: OF EGYPTIANS LIVE ON 5% OF THE LAND

descrizione:
Egypt is one and a half times the size of Texas, yet almost everyone squeezes onto a thin green ribbon along the Nile. Why would a giant country crowd into a strip of mud? We follow the river from the pharaohs to the Aswan High Dam, from bread riots to a brand new capital in the desert, and all the way to a huge dam in Ethiopia.

Every border has a price, and so does every river. Watch how geography, population, debt and water shape the fate of 109 million people, and why the Nile is both Egypt's lifeline and its greatest risk.

scene.testo: A desert giant with one thin green line. A new capital almost nobody lives in. A dam two thousand kilometers away. Why does everyone squeeze in here?
Egypt is huge. It is almost one and a half times the size of Texas. Yet most of it is empty.
Turn off the sun and most of it vanishes. All that is left is one thin line of light, with a flower at the top.
That line is the Nile. Around ninety-five percent of Egypt's 109 million people live along it, on roughly five percent of the land.
So why would a country this big squeeze into a strip this thin? The long answer involves bread riots and a ghost capital.

eventi.testo: Bread, a ghost capital, a dam

scene.testo: It also involves a dam more than two thousand kilometers away, finished in 2025, which Egypt calls a threat to its very existence.
Start with the sky. Cairo gets about two and a half centimeters of rain a year, roughly half of what falls on Death Valley.
No rain means no rivers of your own. Not one permanent river starts inside Egypt. About ninety-seven percent of its water comes from the Nile.
Once it crosses into Egypt, no other river ever joins it. Not one, all the way to the sea.
Everything else is the Sahara. Seas of sand, rocky plateaus, and oases hundreds of kilometers apart.
From space, Egypt looks like a desert with one green thread running through it. Follow that thread and you find almost every farm and most cities.
The ancient Egyptians saw their world the same way. They had two names for it: Kemet, the black land, and Deshet, the red land.
Every summer, heavy rain fell on mountains far to the south. Weeks later, the Nile rose and spilled over the whole valley.
When the water drained away, it left a fresh layer of black mud. Free fertilizer, delivered every single year.
The pharaohs measured the flood with stone staircases called nilometers. Too low and people starved. Too high and villages washed away.
Just right and the harvest was great, and so were the taxes. Pharaohs, Greeks, Romans, Arabs, Ottomans, the British. Rulers came and went. The people stayed.
Then in 1970, Egypt did something no pharaoh ever could. It switched the flood off.
The Aswan High Dam blocked the river with a wall of rock and clay, creating one of the biggest artificial lakes on Earth.
The water rose so high it would have drowned ancient temples. So the world cut Abu Simbel into blocks and moved it up the hill.
No more floods, and no more hungry years when the river ran low. Farmers could now grow two or three crops a year instead of one.
But the mud stopped coming. It now settles at the bottom of the lake, so farmers buy fertilizer instead.

eventi.testo: Mud now sinks behind the dam

scene.testo: And the delta, the land that mud built, is slowly being eaten by the sea.
So that is the short answer. Egyptians live by the Nile because there is nowhere else to get water. The real story is what happens when a nation packs onto one strip of mud.
In 1950, Egypt had about twenty-one million people. Today it has 109 million, and the United Nations expects around 160 million by 2050.
Egypt adds a million people roughly every nine months. That is one more person about every twenty-three seconds.
Nearly all of them have to fit along that one line. All of Egypt's farmland together covers about the area of Switzerland.
Switzerland has nine million people. This land has to feed more than one hundred million.
Greater Cairo alone is home to over twenty million people. With empty desert on both sides, the city can only spread one way, onto the fields.
Building on farmland is illegal in Egypt. People do it anyway. A son gets married, the family needs another floor, and land with a house is worth far more than crops.
In about forty years, Egypt has lost roughly 1700 square kilometers of farmland to illegal buildings. That is more or less the whole city of Houston.
And it is not just any land. It is the black mud the river spent thousands of years laying down.
Here is the trap. More Egyptians need more homes, and every home on the river buries the land meant to feed them.
So Egypt buys food from abroad, a lot of it. It is among the biggest wheat buyers on the planet, about thirteen million tons a year.
Until 2022, most of it came from just two countries, Russia and Ukraine.
You know what happened next. When the war started, wheat prices shot up, and so did Egypt's bill.
Much of that wheat becomes one thing, a round flatbread called aish baladi. In Egyptian Arabic, the word for bread also means life.
Around seventy million Egyptians buy it at a price fixed by the state. And that price is political dynamite.
In 1977, the government tried to raise it. Riots broke out across the country, and within days the president backed down.
For more than thirty years, a subsidized loaf cost the same five piastres. In 2024, the government finally quadrupled it to twenty.
That is still less than half a US cent. So the strip is full, the fields are shrinking, and the bread depends on foreign harvests.
So the government chose one way out: build a second Egypt in the desert. Forty-five kilometers east of Cairo, where there was only sand, there is now this.
Egypt's new capital covers around seven hundred square kilometers, about the size of Singapore. It has the tallest skyscraper in Africa and the biggest cathedral in the Middle East.
The estimated bill is up to 58 billion dollars. In 2023, the ministries moved in, and tens of thousands of workers now commute into the desert.
It is not the only one. The government is building more than twenty new cities and says the inhabited share of Egypt has doubled from seven to fourteen percent.
So did Egyptians finally leave the river? The new capital was planned for six and a half million people. In 2025, its developer said a little over 30,000 lived there.
Egypt's population grows by that much in about eight days. The new capital is a city built for millions that feels like a ghost town.
The reason is simple. The apartments cost far more than a government worker earns, and the jobs, schools and relatives are still back in the valley.
Even the new desert farms cannot escape the river. To water them, Egypt built the largest water treatment plant in the world, a Guinness record.
It cleans dirty drainage water from the delta's fields, water that came from the Nile in the first place, and sends it into the desert.

eventi.testo: Escape from the Nile runs on the Nile

scene.testo: All of this costs money, much of it borrowed in dollars. In 2015, one dollar bought about eight Egyptian pounds. Today it buys around fifty.
For a country that pays for wheat in dollars, almost everything gets more expensive. Shopping for bread means paying a price set abroad.
In 2024, desperate for dollars, Egypt sold the United Arab Emirates the rights to develop a Mediterranean coastline. A deal worth 35 billion dollars.
It was the biggest foreign investment in Egyptian history. Crowded cities, debt, the price of bread: Egypt can at least try to fix these alone.
The last problem it cannot fix, because Egypt's water does not fall in Egypt. Follow the river south, past Aswan, to Khartoum in Sudan.
There two rivers meet. The White Nile is steady, but about half of it evaporates in South Sudan's swamps.
The other, the Blue Nile, crashes down from the mountains of Ethiopia. Remember that summer rain that flooded the valley? This is where it falls.
Around eighty-five percent of the Nile water reaching Egypt starts as rain in Ethiopia. And Egypt has a river whose source it does not own.
In 1959, Egypt and Sudan divided the river between themselves: fifty-five and a half billion cubic meters a year for Egypt, eighteen and a half for Sudan.
Ethiopia got nothing. It was not even part of the deal. So in 2011, it started building the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.
It is Africa's biggest hydroelectric power plant and it took more than a decade. From 2020, Ethiopia filled the lake behind it stage by stage.
That lake can hold 74 billion cubic meters, more than Egypt's entire yearly share of the Nile.
For Ethiopia, this was never really about Egypt. In 2023, almost half of Ethiopians still had no electricity.
Ethiopia paid for most of the dam itself, partly with bonds bought by ordinary citizens. And it now has some 135 million people, more than Egypt.
Egypt sees it very differently. Its foreign minister told the UN Security Council the dam was an existential threat.
In September 2025, Ethiopia officially inaugurated the dam. Within weeks, the river flooded villages in Sudan and even in Egypt's delta.
Egypt blamed sudden, unannounced releases from the dam. Ethiopia said the dam had actually made the flood smaller. Same river, same water, two stories.
But the real fear in Cairo is not a flood. It is a drought. If dry years come back to back, a dam in another country decides how much flows down.
And there is still no binding agreement on the rules. Egypt's best protection is, ironically, its own dam.

eventi.testo: No binding deal on filling rules

scene.testo: The lake behind Aswan is one of the largest reservoirs on Earth, a savings account for dry years. The dam that switched off the flood is now Egypt's insurance policy.
Even so, the math is worrying. Egypt's yearly water divided by its people comes to about 500 cubic meters each, right at the UN line for absolute scarcity.
Compare that with a thousand cubic meters, the point where a country is already called water stressed. Egypt sits at half of even that.
So the scorecard. Geography: a river through a desert, which gave Egypt everything and nowhere else to go. History: fifty centuries on one strip of mud.
Decisions: taming the river and building cities few people moved to. And one source of water that Egypt does not control.

eventi.testo: Water source not in its hands

scene.testo: Why does everyone live here? Because this thin green line is the only place in Egypt where the desert lets people live.
Since this video began, Egypt has gained more than two dozen people, and almost every one of them will live right here.

eventi.testo: Almost all will live on the Nile

scene.testo: A country can be as big as Texas, yet if only a ribbon of it has water, that ribbon is the whole country.
